original_risk: The core workflow remains too complex for a first-time team.
A new team cannot reach its first useful run in five minutes.
The CLI is missing or too awkward, so developers avoid the product.
There is no strong IDE/editor integration where developers already work.
Repository indexing and context selection miss important files or decisions.
Long sessions lose context or produce inconsistent handoffs.
Resume, retry, rollback, and checkpoint behavior is confusing or unreliable.
Review and pull-request workflows feel bolted on rather than native.
Agents lack safe branch/worktree isolation for concurrent work.
The product handles coding runs but not adjacent planning, testing, documentation, or incident workflows.
Prompt injection arrives through repository files, issues, pull requests, documents, or tool output.
Agents expose API keys, tokens, secrets, or proprietary source code.
A sandbox escape or unsafe network path turns an agent run into host compromise.
Malicious MCP servers, skills, plugins, or dependencies enter through the agent supply chain.
Permissions are too broad, so a “read-only” workflow can still change files or call external systems.
A compromised or malicious model provider returns instructions that bypass the intended workflow.
A cross-tenant authorization bug exposes another team’s runs, events, files, or costs.
Personal-key sharing creates unclear consent, ownership, billing, or revocation behavior.
OAuth, webhooks, email login, or session handling fails under real production attacks.
The product cannot produce sufficient security evidence for a customer’s review, procurement, or insurance requirements.
Provider outages, rate limits, or model quotas stop customer runs.
Model updates silently change behavior and invalidate plans, tests, or review results.
Long-running runs fail after consuming tokens without a usable resume point.
Queue, concurrency, or cancellation bugs cause starvation, duplicate work, or runaway spend.
Multi-replica deployment breaks sessions, WebSockets, OAuth state, rate limits, or event ordering.
Event logs, indexes, artifacts, or databases grow until storage and query costs become serious.
Backups exist but a real restore has never been proven under pressure.
Missing or noisy traces make customer incidents impossible to diagnose.
Different model, prompt, contract, or dependency versions make results irreproducible.
A vulnerable dependency, container, image, or build tool creates an emergency release.
Buyers cannot see a measurable return on investment beyond “the agent feels useful.”
Developers distrust the system and bypass it with direct Claude, Cursor, Codex, or local-agent usage.
Engineering managers do not want another dashboard or approval ceremony.
The team uses the Harness only for demos and not for recurring production work.
GitHub, GitLab, IDEs, and agent providers change APIs faster than integrations can keep up.
GitHub, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, or Microsoft bundle similar governance into tools customers already pay for.
The category is too crowded and the phrase “AI engineering harness” is not understood by buyers.
Enterprise security and procurement reviews take longer than the product’s sales runway.
Self-hosted installation, upgrades, backups, and provider setup are too difficult for ordinary teams.
Documentation, examples, support, and community are too thin to create independent adoption.
Model and infrastructure costs exceed subscription revenue when teams run many agents.
Pricing is guessed, underpriced, or too complicated to explain.
Every customer requires custom deployment and support, turning SaaS into unprofitable consulting.
Teams value governance but are not willing to pay for it separately from their existing agent tools.
Shared credentials make it impossible to attribute spend and protect the key owner from surprise bills.
A customer blames the Harness for an agent-generated defect, data loss, outage, or security incident.
Data residency, privacy, retention, or sector compliance requirements block otherwise interested customers.
Provider terms, model access rules, or third-party API policies restrict the BYO-key or multi-provider model.
Usage falls after the initial novelty period because the team has no recurring trigger to return.
The best features are copied or absorbed by larger platforms before the Harness establishes distribution, workflow data, or customer trust.
